newsitem.title: USA: Coffee and oil prices fall, platinum soars.
newsitem.headline: Coffee and oil prices fall, platinum soars.

text.p: Coffee prices fell sharply for a second straight day on Thursday as both commercial coffee firms and speculators sold on easing concerns about supply shortages this summer.

"The near-term psychology has changed," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "Colombia is indicating to exporters, go sell what you can. And Brazil exports are already way ahead of last year," he added.

Coffee for July delivery at the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange fell 21.05 cents or more than eight percent to close at 230.50 cents a pound, down sharply from the 20-year high of 318 cents a pound set one week earlier.
Lack of any damaging cold to Brazil's coffee trees so far at the onset of winter there has eased fears that next year's production might be damaged by frost, as occurred in 1994.
So news out of second-largest producer Colombia since late last week continued to weigh on sentiment.
Colombian exporters last week said they were having a hard time finding buyers for about 300,000 bags of coffee for June shipment because of high prices.
Each bag contains 132 pounds of green coffee beans.

On Tuesday, Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said the country had opened "unlimited" coffee registrations for July to August, a period in which he said Colombia planned to sell up to 2.5 million bags of coffee.

The International Coffee Organization said on Thursday that its exporting members' shipments rose to 50.07 million bags in the first seven months of the current coffee year ending in April, up from 43.49 million a year earlier.
Brazil's exports in April alone were 1.4 million bags compared to 732,000 bags a year earlier, underscoring the push producers have made since December to cash in on high prices.

Elsewhere, platinum prices soared amid talk of very tight cash market supplies tied to the five-month suspension of exports by Russia, the world's largest supplier of platinum group metals (PGMs) that also include palladium.
Platinum for July delivery at the New York Mercantile Exchange closed up the daily allowable limit of $25 an ounce at $436.60 an ounce, a new life-of-contract high.
Cash platinum in London earlier on Thursday was fixed at $440.00, the highest price since September 15, 1995.
"The fundamentals in PGMs look strong, the technicals look strong, the funds are still buying platinum and few people want to sell it," Pioneer Futures analyst Scott Meyers said.

June palladium set a life-of-contract high at $214 an ounce before falling to close at $200.15, down $2.65. Traders said talk of possible defaults on cash market deliveries had unnerved some buyers of futures, prompting the sales.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for July delivery closed 6 cents a bushel higher at $8.36 on talk that China was interested in buying and ideas that supplies will continue to be tight despite some soybean imports from South America.

"The commercial buying we've seen is tied to the need to find some beans," said Jack Scoville, analyst with The Price Group brokerage. "These guys need beans otherwise Cargill wouldn't be importing five cargos from Brazil."
On Wednesday, Cargill Inc said tight supplies of U.S. soybeans had forced the company to contract for an unspecified quantity of Brazilian soybeans.
July wheat rose 2-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $3.56.

"I think people are making a case that the wheat is bottoming out, because it usually does at this time of year," said Scoville. "Also, we've got rain in the forecast for the weekend which could keep cutting slow. There's talk of disease starting to pick up in the soft red crops," he added.
Wheat harvesting in Texas has been progressing but cash dealers have given mixed reviews to early yields and quality.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices fell for a third straight day as increasing domestic supply and the prospect of another $2 billion worth of Iraqi oil to be sold over the next six months continued to weigh on prices.
"There is a general sense that storage levels are rising and that crude does not deserve a premium given the supply situation," said trader Mike De Luca at Prudential Securities.

Crude for July delivery closed 46 cents lower at $19.66 a barrel. Refined products followed the lead of crude with July July heating oil ending down 0.84 cent at 53.32 cents a gallon and July gasoline down 0.60 cent at 59.82 cents a gallon.

The American Petroleum Institute said on Tuesday that for the week ended May 30 gasoline output stood at 8.195 million barrels a day, a record high. The same data showed domestic crude stocks swelling by 8.4 million barrels.

On Wednesday, the United Nations Security Council formally renewed an "oil-for-food" accord with Iraq. Under the deal, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude oil for six months in order to buy food, medicine and other supplies.
